readiness.mainReason: No blocking rule fired: the decision is clear, the core recommendation is supported and sourced, the framing holds and the load-bearing assumptions and risks are stated, so the residual findings refine the plan without changing the launch decision.
readiness.highestRiskIssue: The full-launch gate on slide 10 clears at 5% while the year-one target on slide 8 is 8%, so the go decision does not confirm the number the case rests on.
readiness.whatCouldChangeIt: Conversion data from the soft launch, the pounds size of the grant income at risk or confirmation that the 5% gate and the 8% target measure the same population would firm up the level. None of these lowers it below Nearly ready on the text as written.

dimensions.name: Client decision usefulness
dimensions.note: The decision, the answer and the first action are stated plainly and early on slides 1, 2 and 10.

dimensions.name: Problem framing
dimensions.note: The membership question is specific, bounded to a single-tier start and held consistently, with a conversion and revenue success measure.

dimensions.name: Storyline and pyramid logic
dimensions.note: Governing insight is up front and every section supports it, but several titles are labels so the titles-only read is weaker than the slide 1 assertion.

dimensions.name: Evidence quality
dimensions.note: Grant share, mailing list, attendance and comparator pricing all carry named sources and the key assumption is flagged as the thing to test.

dimensions.name: Analysis and insight
dimensions.note: Evidence is interpreted into implications, the single-tier alternative is compared and findings feed the recommendation.

dimensions.name: Recommendation specificity
dimensions.note: The action, the owner, the timing and a measurable target are all named on slides 6, 8 and 10.

dimensions.name: Feasibility and implementation
dimensions.note: The plan is sized to the client and sequenced with a pilot, but the partner-discount dependency on slide 7 is not acknowledged as an external agreement.

dimensions.name: Risks, assumptions and uncertainty
dimensions.note: Load-bearing assumptions and the main risk are named, the tier tradeoff is acknowledged and uncertainty is stated honestly.

dimensions.name: Slide-level communication
dimensions.note: Each slide carries one message and content matches the title, but several content titles are topic labels rather than assertions.

dimensions.name: Professionalism, tone and confidentiality
dimensions.note: Tone is fit for a client, no named individual is judged (the coordinator is a role) and certainty is appropriate.

strengths.point: The deck answers first: the title and slide 2 state the decision and the answer before the evidence.
strengths.quote: Our answer is yes, with a deliberately small start.

strengths.point: The load-bearing assumption is named as the thing to test rather than hidden.
strengths.quote: The 8% assumption is conservative against the 32% attendance rate and is the main thing to test.

strengths.point: The first steps are concrete, owned and sequenced.
strengths.quote: The Client E coordinator owns the launch.
Project grants are 80% of Client E's income (2024 accounts) and each is single-year.

findings.title: The full-launch gate is set at 5% while the stated year-one target is 8%, so the go decision does not test the number the plan rests on.
findings.principle: Internal consistency: the go/no-go gate must match the target the plan is built on.
findings.diagnosis: Slide 8 builds the year-one revenue of about 5,000 pounds on an 8% conversion and calls 8% the main thing to test. Slide 10 reviews against that 8% target in month two but full launches in month three if the soft launch clears only 5%. The soft launch goes to the most engaged 200 contacts, who should convert above the full-list rate, so a 5% bar on that group does not confirm the 8% full-list assumption and lets a full launch proceed at a conversion that misses the 5,000 pounds the case cites.

evidence.quote: If 8% of the mailing list joins at 45 pounds, that is about 5,000 pounds in year one.
Month two: review conversion against the 8% target. Month three: full launch if the soft launch clears 5%.

findings.why: If conversion lands between 5% and 8% the plan still triggers a full launch, but year-one income comes in below the 5,000 pounds the deck used to justify the scheme, so the client acts on a number the gate never validated.
findings.reflect: What conversion rate on the most engaged 200 would actually confirm an 8% rate across the full list, and is that the number the gate should use.
findings.fix: Align the go gate with the target: derive the soft-launch pass mark from what an 8% full-list rate implies for the most engaged 200 or restate the year-one revenue at the 5% the gate accepts. Make the two thresholds tell one story.

findings.title: The deck shows grants at risk but never sizes the shortfall, so the reader cannot judge whether the membership target meaningfully diversifies income.
findings.principle: Analysis: a diversification case has to size the gap it is filling.
findings.diagnosis: Slide 3 says project grants are 80% of income and two of five are not expected to renew. Slide 8 sets a year-one target of about 5,000 pounds. The deck never states the pounds of grant income at risk, so a reader cannot tell whether 5,000 pounds is a meaningful start against the gap or a rounding error, even granting that the start is deliberately small.

evidence.quote: Two of five grants are not expected to renew, per the funder letters on file.
If 8% of the mailing list joins at 45 pounds, that is about 5,000 pounds in year one.

findings.why: A funder or board member weighing the scheme will ask how far 5,000 pounds goes against the income it is meant to replace, and the deck gives no way to answer.
findings.reflect: How many pounds of grant income are at risk over the next two years, and what share does the year-one and scaled membership target cover.
findings.fix: Add the pounds at risk from the non-renewing grants and set the membership target against it, so the small start reads as a first step toward a sized gap rather than an unbenchmarked figure.

findings.title: The member discount with local partners is presented as existing capacity, but it depends on partner agreements the deck does not evidence.
findings.principle: Feasibility: a promised benefit that needs a third party is a dependency, not existing capacity.
findings.diagnosis: Slide 7 lists a discount with local partners among the member benefits and then says these use capacity Client E already has. Priority booking and members-only events are within Client E's control, but a partner discount needs those partners to agree, which the deck does not evidence.

evidence.quote: Priority booking, two members-only events a year and a discount with local partners.
These use capacity Client E already has.

findings.why: If the partner discounts are not secured before launch, the membership offer is thinner than advertised and early members may feel short-changed.
findings.reflect: Which local partners have agreed to a member discount, and what is the fallback offer if none have by launch.
findings.fix: Separate the benefits Client E controls from the partner discount, and either confirm the partner agreements before launch or drop the discount from the launch offer until it is secured.

comments.problem: Several content titles are topic labels ("The decision", "The numbers", "First steps") while slide 1 shows the assertive style.
comments.why: A board member skimming only the titles gets the answer from slide 1 but not the reasoning, so the titles-only read is weaker than it could be.
comments.fix: Rewrite the label titles as full-sentence takeaways in the slide 1 style.

comments.problem: Client E prices at 45 pounds, the low end of the 40 to 60 pounds comparators, with no reason given.
comments.why: A reader may wonder whether 45 pounds leaves money on the table or reflects a deliberate conversion play.
comments.fix: Add one line on why 45 pounds: single tier, conversion-first or a deliberate entry price.

questionsForLead: Why is the full-launch gate 5% when the year-one target is 8%, and is the 5% measured on the most engaged 200 or on the full list.
How much grant income in pounds is at risk over the next two years, so the 5,000 pound target can be judged against it.
Have any local partners agreed to offer the member discount, or is that still to be secured.
Is the 1,400 person mailing list consented for membership marketing under GDPR.

learningNote.lesson: A success target and the gate you use to act on it must be the same number. When the review threshold and the go threshold differ, the plan can proceed on a result it told itself was not good enough.
learningNote.weakHabit: Setting a headline target then quietly gating the decision at a lower, easier bar.
learningNote.exercise: For the next plan, write the go/no-go rule first, then check that every target quoted elsewhere in the deck is the number that rule actually uses. Reconcile any that differ.

notAssessed: Whether the 8% conversion assumption holds. No conversion data was provided and the team names it as the main thing to test.
The pounds of grant income at risk. The deck gives the 80% share but not the amount.
Whether local partners have agreed to the member discount. Not evidenced in the deck.
Whether the 1,400 person mailing list is accurate and consented for marketing. Stated as an assumption, not verified.
Visual design, layout and charts. Only slide text was provided.
